newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian debt more than ready for RBA to move.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt more than ready for RBA to move.

text.p: *The Australian debt market is more than prepared for a monetary policy easing on Friday following Thursday's weaker than expected wages.
*Ten-year bond futures set all-time high of 93.640.

The Australian debt market is more than prepared for a monetary policy easing on Friday following Thursday's weaker than expected wages data, but the risk is the RBA will wait until after the August board meeting.

The 10-year bond futures contract squeezed out an all-time-high of 93.640 at one stage, taking the 10-year bond yield below 6.40 percent and its lowest level since Australian financial markets were deregulated in the early 1980s.
The market rallied across the curve after second quarter wages growth rose just 0.5 percent for an annual 3.7 percent.
Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank, described the data as "breathtaking".
"If anything it looks too good to be true. The 0.5 percent rise in wages was well below what we expected but adds to the case for a further rate cut," he added.
The data follows hot on the heels of Wednesday's extremely subdued inflation report which saw the policy sensitive underlying rate at its lowest level since 1971 at 1.7 percent.
The September bill futures contract touched a high of 94.98 on the data, which equates to a cash rate of 5.02 percent compared with current 5.5 percent official interest rates.

"Another way of looking at this is that by pricing in 48 basis points of an expected 50 basis points easing, the market is attaching a 96 percent probability on a near term rate cut," said Glenn Maguire, economist at Societe Generale.
However, such has been the run of data been this week, there has been some discussion of the possibility of a larger rate cut to stimulate the economy.

"Will the cut be 50 basis points or 75 basis points," Colonial's Kunnen said. "A cut of 50 points will start speculation of yet another cut. A more decisive cut now would signal and end to this series of rate cuts."
The market's rally saw it make a strong test of 25 basis points on the Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread, also its lowest level since the early 1980s.

There are mixed opinions as to whether this margin can compress any further, although today's wages data is seen confirming Australia's low inflation performance which is currently far better than the of U.S., analysts noted.
Wednesday's data showed the annual headline inflation rate stands at just 0.3 percent, while the U.S. stands at 2.3 percent.

U.S. Treasuries stayed around their New York price lows in Tokyo trade, having given up some ground after Tuesday's heady rally, while Canadian debt underperformed as it absorbed the supply of a C$1.3 billion 30-year bond auction. The N.Z. short end outshone the bloc as the N.Z. dollar rallied.

The 10-year bond's all-time high of 93.640 overtook the previous peak of 93.630 set in early 1994. The market has now fully retraced the sell-off that followed that peak during the rest of 1994 which resulted in a fall to 89.140 by November.
